title: Two Thousand Dollars and a Barn: Wilson Greatbatch's Pacemaker Years
dek: In 1958 an engineer in Buffalo quit his jobs, handed his savings to his wife and spent two years building implantable pacemakers in the barn behind his house.

story.company: Wilson Greatbatch's barn workshop (later Wilson Greatbatch Ltd)
story.event: Quitting his jobs to build implantable pacemakers by hand in his barn, 1958 to 1960
story.summary: After a first implantable pacemaker ran in a dog at the Buffalo Veterans Administration hospital on 7 May 1958, Wilson Greatbatch quit his jobs and, living on $2,000 in savings, hand-built fifty pacemakers in the barn behind his house in Clarence, New York, over two years. From April 1960 the surgeon William Chardack implanted them in ten patients, and the device was licensed to Medtronic. Short battery life led Greatbatch to a lithium battery and, in 1970, his own company.
paragraphs: In 1958 Wilson Greatbatch was making a living in Buffalo, New York, from more than one job, including managing an electronics division at Taber Instrument and teaching electrical engineering at the University of Buffalo. Two years earlier, building a circuit to record heart sounds, he had fitted a resistor of the wrong size. The circuit went blip, waited a second, and went blip again. "Oh that's a pacemaker," he recalled thinking.

What he knew was mostly discouraging. Pacemakers of the day stayed outside the body: Paul Zoll's in Boston plugged into the wall, and the belt-worn units his friend Earl Bakken built in Minneapolis ran wires through the skin. For two years, he said, Buffalo doctors told him patients with complete heart block "die in two years. There is nothing you can do about it." Then William Chardack, chief of surgery at the Veterans Administration hospital, paced his dog laboratory and told him that if he could do it, he could save ten thousand lives a year. On 7 May 1958 their first model, wrapped in electrical tape, ran in a dog for about four hours before body fluids got in and shorted it.

Taber would not take on the legal risk of an unproven implant, and no manufacturer was interested. So, by his own account, to his wife's consternation he quit all his jobs. He had $2,000 in cash, enough to keep the family for two years. He gave it to his wife, Eleanor, and went up to the wood-heated barn behind their house in Clarence. In two years he built fifty pacemakers by hand, learning to cast the circuits in solid epoxy after the tape failed.

In April 1960 Chardack implanted the first of ten in patients, two of them children; the first patient's pacemaker ran for eighteen months. The mercury batteries were the weak point. Their maker said six years, and few lasted more than two. Once there were ten successful patients, Greatbatch licensed the pacemaker to Medtronic. A decade later he developed a long-lived lithium battery and founded his own company, Wilson Greatbatch Ltd, to make batteries for pacemakers.

quote.text: The man of virtue makes the difficulty to be overcome his first business, and success only a subsequent consideration;-- this may be called perfect virtue.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Confucius puts the difficulty first and success after it. Greatbatch spent two years on the hardest part, sealing a working circuit inside a living body, before anyone would pay for it. The passage does not say who carries the cost while success waits; in the barn, it was his family.

reflection: Greatbatch's two years were not a leap into the dark. He knew how much money there was, how long it would last and who was holding it. He handed the savings to his wife and kept the work, which put a limit on the risk and a witness beside it.

You may be weighing how far to go with your own work, and at whose cost. Putting the difficulty first, as Confucius asks, does not mean carrying it alone or without an end date. Fifty pacemakers were built in that barn before ten went into patients, and someone at home knew exactly how long the money had to last.
invitation: Tell one person at home how long you are prepared to give the hardest part of your work, and what you will look at when that time is up.

research_notes: Leaving work: Greatbatch's 2000 oral history says he 'quit all my jobs'; MIT Technology Review says Taber Instrument declined the liability and he 'set out on his own' with $2,000; the NAE tribute says only that Taber did not support the research and he continued independently. The story uses his own account and the Taber refusal. Medtronic licence year: MIT Technology Review says 1960 and the oral history implies 1960 ('we essentially gave them patients'), while the NAE tribute says 1961; the story gives no year and dates it by his account ('once there were ten successful patients'). Battery life: he says Mallory insisted on publishing six years but few batteries ran more than two; MIT Technology Review describes the lithium battery as extending life from two to ten years; the story uses his figures. Resistor date: MIT Technology Review, UB and the NAE give 1956; Lemelson-MIT says 'late 1950s'; the story says two years before 1958. Patients: MIT Technology Review says Chardack implanted the first of ten in April 1960; the NAE adds that two were children; the oral history says the first patient's pacemaker ran eighteen months, without naming the patient, so no patient details are added. The often-quoted line about his 'elation' when the pacemaker took control of a heart comes from his later book, which could not be read online, so it is not used. Chardack's words are paraphrased because they reach the story only through Greatbatch's memory. The company field names the barn workshop because Wilson Greatbatch Ltd did not exist until 1970; the pacemaker itself was licensed to Medtronic.
